periods.activity_title: Entering the World of Para-Sport: First Impressions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.137): observe Sheetal Devi image, share impressions, write caption
Reflect and Respond (p.138): K-W-L table on Paralympics — what I know, want to know

time_bands.activity: Open by displaying the image of Sheetal Devi on the board. Students observe silently, then share initial impressions with a partner before a brief whole-class share-out. Draw out observations about sporting posture, equipment, and the significance of the Arjuna Award.

Students give a caption for the image in their notebooks and volunteer readings aloud. Collect a range of captions on the board to show how interpretation varies; prompt students to consider what qualities the captions highlight.

Introduce the K-W-L table from Reflect and Respond. Students fill in the 'What I know' column individually, then pair-share before attempting 'What I want to know'. Collect recurring 'Want to know' questions on the board as a reading purpose-setter.

Teacher reads aloud the chapter title and the chapter's opening paragraph (p.137–138), modelling expressive reading of an informational text. Students follow in their textbooks and flag one word or phrase that strikes them as significant.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening encounter with para-sport and disability advocacy, so activating students' existing knowledge and curiosity is the priority before any reading begins. The image of Sheetal Devi, a limb-different para-archer, is likely to surface mixed reactions — allow respectful discussion without directing students toward a 'correct' emotional response. Note any misconceptions about disability that surface in the K-W-L table for gentle correction as reading proceeds.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Interview: Dr. Deepa Malik's Journey

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.143): fact table on Dr. Malik — diagnosis, surgery, awards, firsts, support

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a shared reading of the interview text (p.138–143), assigning student volunteers to read the interviewer's questions and Dr. Malik's responses in turns. Pause at key moments — the spinal tumour diagnosis, the two-choices passage, the Rio 2016 silver — to allow brief unscripted reactions from the class.

Students work individually to complete the fact table from Reading for Meaning (p.143): age at diagnosis, result of surgery, the body that recognised her globally, her first successful event, her two 'firsts', her three awards, and two causes she supports. Students then compare answers in pairs.

Whole-class verification of the fact table, with teacher writing agreed answers on the board. Highlight that 'firsts' and 'awards' must be precise — generalising is a common error in informational reading. Invite one student to state in a single sentence what makes Dr. Malik's story distinctive.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate Dr. Malik's awards (Khel Ratna, Arjuna, Padma Shri) and may list them in wrong order or omit one; slow down at that fact-table row. Her two stated 'firsts' — first Indian female para-athlete to win an Asian Games athletics medal, and India's first female Paralympic medallist in any sport — are distinct claims and both must be recorded separately.

periods.activity_title: Fact, Opinion, Cause and Effect in Dr. Malik's Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.143–144): identify fact-opinion or cause-effect in two sentence sets
Check Your Understanding (p.144): pair work — classify two more sentence pairs as cause-effect or fact-opinion

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly distinguishes fact, opinion, cause, and effect on the board using two neutral examples unrelated to the chapter. Students suggest one more example of each type to confirm understanding before applying the distinctions to Dr. Malik's words.

Students work individually on the two sentence sets from Check Your Understanding (p.143–144) — the Rio silver and the tumour diagnosis — identifying whether each set is fact-opinion or cause-effect. Responses are shared aloud and unpacked: what linguistic signals (e.g. 'I feel', 'was told') cue the distinction.

Pair work on the second set of sentence pairs (p.144) featuring Dr. Malik's Five-Year Plan membership and the Paralympics-perception link. Pairs write 1 (cause-effect) or 2 (fact-opinion) in their books and justify their choice with one sentence. Quick whole-class check closes the activity.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often misidentify an opinion as a fact when the speaker is an authority figure; draw attention to hedging phrases ('I feel', 'it is believed') as reliable opinion markers. The Five-Year Plan sentence pair is the harder one because both sentences are declarative — prompt students to ask 'does the first make the second happen?' to test for cause-effect.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading Extract 1: The Caterpillar Transformation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.145): Extract 1 — caterpillar analogy, para-athletics transition, 'in hindsight', 'changing perceptions'

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 aloud (p.145) while students follow. Students re-read it silently and underline words or phrases that seem to carry particular weight: 'squander', 'remorse', 'breakthrough', 'in hindsight', 'changing perceptions'.

Students answer all five questions from Critical Reflection (p.145) in sequence, writing responses in their notebooks. The caterpillar-analogy SCR, the swimming-background SCR, the 'breakthrough moment' fill-in, the 'in hindsight' MCQ, and the 'changing perceptions' SCR are worked through one by one, with students sharing answers after each before moving on.

Whole-class discussion: teacher asks students to explain, in their own words, what Dr. Malik means by 'a step forward in changing perceptions' — whose perceptions, changed how, about what. Students respond orally; teacher annotates key ideas on the board to consolidate the extract's main argument.

periods.teacher_notes: The caterpillar analogy question asks students to reason by analogy — a skill that requires them to map the transformation (paralysis → para-athlete) onto the metamorphosis (caterpillar → butterfly); students who focus only on the outcome miss the hidden struggle stage. The word 'hindsight' is often guessed incorrectly as 'courage' or 'determination' — draw attention to its temporal meaning: looking back after the event.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading Extract 2: Breaking Stereotypes and Pushing Boundaries

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.146): Extract 2 — tone identification, analogy, true-false, 'push boundaries', life-transformation phrase

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 2 aloud (p.146) expressively, then invites two student volunteers to re-read it with attention to tone. The class listens and notes, without writing, what emotional quality they detect in the speaker's voice.

Students work through all five sub-questions from Critical Reflection (p.146) independently: the tone MCQ (selecting from appreciative, moralistic, sentimental, optimistic, defensive), the analogy fill-in, the true-false statement, the 'push boundaries' SCR, and the phrase-identification task. After each question teacher invites two or three student answers and unpacks why distractors are plausible.

Consolidation: teacher asks students to compose, in one written sentence, the central claim of Extract 2 in their own words — not quoting Dr. Malik but paraphrasing her argument. Two or three are read aloud and briefly evaluated for accuracy and register.

periods.teacher_notes: The tone MCQ is the item students find hardest — 'sentimental' and 'moralistic' are attractive distractors because Dr. Malik does speak passionately and approvingly; guide students to look for what the speaker is trying to do (advocate, inspire) rather than how she feels. The analogy item ('ability : potential :: preconceived notions : ___') requires students to identify the relationship as 'both terms refer to inner resource or fixed assumption' — the target word 'stereotypes' is in the extract.

periods.activity_title: Analytical Discussion: Title Justification and Life Lessons

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.146–147): seven extended-answer questions — title justification, societal impact, gender equality, life lessons

time_bands.activity: Teacher assigns the seven extended-answer questions (p.146–147) and divides them across small groups of three: each group drafts written responses to two or three questions as assigned. Students work in their notebooks, drawing on the whole interview text read in earlier encounters.

Groups share their responses question by question in a jigsaw-style whole-class discussion. For the title-justification question, teacher invites competing justifications before arriving at a class consensus. For the gender-equality question, teacher asks students to name one structural barrier Dr. Malik's career disrupts.

Individual writing: students write three to four sentences in response to the final question — what they have learnt and how they might apply it — as a personal reflection rather than a textbook answer. Two volunteers read their reflections aloud and the class responds with a single appreciative observation each.

periods.teacher_notes: The title-justification question is the chapter's most synthetic close-reading demand: students must connect Dr. Malik's specific choices and achievements to the abstract phrase 'limitless possibilities' — push them beyond 'she worked hard' to name the philosophical claim the title makes. The question on gender equality in sports is also asking students to think structurally, not just list achievements; a useful prompt is 'what assumption does her story disprove?'

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary in Motion: Phrases, Word Clines, and Modal Verbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.147): match five idiomatic phrases to meanings, then use each in an original sentence
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.148): arrange eleven movement words on a pace cline, slowest to fastest
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.148): match four modal-verb sentences to their grammatical functions

time_bands.activity: Pair work on the phrase-matching task (p.147): students match 'defy the odds', 'a new lease of life', 'in hindsight', 'breakthrough moment', and 'turn obstacles into stepping stones' to their meanings. Pairs then compose one original sentence each using their chosen phrase, ensuring the meaning is demonstrably used — not just inserted.

Individual work on the word-cline task (p.148): students arrange all eleven movement words from crawl to sprint in increasing pace. Whole-class check on the board reveals that 'amble', 'saunter', and 'stroll' cluster at slow-medium and students often dispute their relative order — teacher explains connotation differences.

Whole-class work on the modal-verb matching task (p.148): teacher reads each of the four sentences aloud, students identify the modal and propose its function before checking against Column 2. Teacher highlights that 'could' here marks past ability — not present possibility — and contrasts it with its other uses listed in the table.

periods.teacher_notes: The idiomatic phrases in this chapter ('defy the odds', 'a new lease of life') are likely to be new to most students; insist that the sentences students produce demonstrate comprehension of the phrase's meaning, not just syntactic placement. The word cline often produces disagreement between 'saunter' and 'stroll' — both are leisurely, but 'saunter' implies a confident, carefree air, while 'stroll' is simply unhurried; acknowledging the partial overlap builds genuine vocabulary sensitivity.

periods.activity_title: Grammar in Context: Modal Functions and Reported Speech

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.149): write nine sentences demonstrating each modal-auxiliary function in context
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.149–150): identify speech type and sentence type; note direct-to-reported speech changes in Column 3

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.151): convert the Siya–Tarun conversation to reported speech, four blanks

time_bands.activity: Students write nine sentences (p.149) — one for each modal function listed in the table: could (possibility, unreal ability, request, suggestion), couldn't (inability), should (probability, advice), would (request, past habit) — labelling the function in brackets after each sentence. Teacher circulates and redirects sentences where the function is not clearly demonstrated by context.

Teacher writes the three direct-speech examples from p.149–150 on the board and students identify speech type (direct) and sentence type (declarative). Students then complete Column 3 — noting the grammatical changes: pronoun shift, tense backshift, reporting verb — for each of the three examples, with the first done together as a model.

Teacher introduces the Siya–Tarun conversation (p.151) as homework: students read it silently, identify the pattern, and are asked to convert it fully to reported speech at home with four blanks completed. Teacher invites one student to convert the first exchange orally as a demonstration before the close.

periods.teacher_notes: The nine-sentence modal task often produces sentences that are grammatically correct but contextually thin — push students to set each sentence in the world of para-sport or everyday school life so the function is unmistakable. For reported speech, the most common error is forgetting pronoun shifts when Dr. Malik speaks in first person ('I' → 'she'); draw attention to this before students attempt Column 3 independently.

periods.activity_title: Listening to an Announcement; Conducting Interviews

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.152): school announcement — fill five blanks with one or two exact words
Speaking Activity (p.152–153): paired interviews — informal with Sports Captain prompts, formal with Sports Coach prompts

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the World Inclusion Day announcement transcript aloud twice at natural speaking pace while students listen for information to fill the five blanks on p.152. On the second reading students write their answers. Whole-class check follows: teacher reads each blank's answer and students verify against what they heard.

Brief whole-class discussion: what distinguishes a formal interview from an informal one? Students name two or three features each — register, mode of address, question phrasing — before moving into pair work.

Pair work on Speaking Activity (p.152–153): partners conduct the informal interview of the Sports Captain using the given prompts, then swap roles and conduct the formal interview of the Sports Coach. Teacher circulates and notes register shifts, then invites one pair to perform each interview type for the class with brief feedback on formality.

periods.teacher_notes: For the listening task, the most common error is mishearing 'Interact Club' as 'interact group' or 'drama club'; play or read the sentence a third time for students who leave that blank empty. For the speaking task, students often drift into informal register during the 'formal' Sports Coach interview — prompt them to notice 'Could you tell me…' versus 'Tell me about…' as a register signal.

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Notice; Launching a Paralympic Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.154): draft a notice (max 50 words, boxed) for an Inter-school Athletic Meet — all required notice elements
Learning Beyond the Text (p.154): form groups, choose presentation topic, plan slide structure and assign roles

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the structure of a formal notice on the board — Organisation, NOTICE heading, date, heading, body, name, designation — using a generic example. Students identify each element and note that the word limit (50 words maximum) requires deliberate concision.

Students draft the Sports Club notice (p.154) independently in their notebooks, drawing a box around the finished text. Two volunteers read their notices aloud; the class checks whether all mandatory elements are present and whether the word count is respected. Teacher gives brief verbal feedback on format and language register.

Students form groups of four for the Learning Beyond the Text project (p.154). Groups choose their topic (lesser-known Paralympic sports or Paralympians from India), read the 'Did you know?' background text, divide the required slides among members, and make an initial note of the sources they will consult. Groups record their division of work in their notebooks before the close.

periods.teacher_notes: Notice writing frequently breaks down when students treat the word limit as approximate — reinforce that exceeding 50 words is a format error in functional writing, and that concision is a skill being assessed, not a formality. For the group project, ensure every group member has a named slide responsibility before the close so that research and preparation are genuinely distributed.

periods.activity_title: Ability Beyond Disability: A Whole-Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Whole-class recall: teacher poses three rapid questions drawing on the chapter's content — Dr. Malik's philosophy, the distinction between fact and opinion in her interview, and one modal verb function from the grammar cluster. Students respond orally, with no written preparation, to consolidate what the chapter has established.

Structured debate: the class divides into two sides to argue the motion 'Paralympic achievement changes social attitudes more effectively than legislation'. Each side has time to prepare two or three points drawing on Dr. Malik's advocacy work, the Paralympic movement's history, and the World Inclusion Day announcement. A student chair manages turns.

Comparative reflection: students write six to eight sentences comparing two dimensions of Dr. Malik's story — her private transformation (choosing possibility over remorse) and her public role (advocacy, equipment provision, school outreach) — using at least two of the chapter's idiomatic phrases ('defy the odds', 'a new lease of life', 'ability beyond disability') correctly in context.

Students form the project groups from Learning Beyond the Text and share, in two minutes per group, the topic they chose and one key fact they have already identified. This is a brief group-voice check rather than a full presentation — each member names one thing they are contributing. Teacher gives one observation per group.

Teacher closes the chapter by returning to the K-W-L table students began in the opening encounter with the text. Students add one or two entries to a third column — 'What I have learnt' — in their notebooks. Teacher reads two aloud to mark the arc from first impressions to informed understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together Dr. Malik's dual identity — para-athlete and disability advocate — that runs through the full interview; students who missed any section of the text can engage through the debate and comparison tasks, which foreground reasoning over recall. The debate motion is deliberately open-ended: students who find 'legislation' under-defined should be encouraged to name a specific law or policy they know, which also surfaces interdisciplinary awareness.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, evaluates authorial purpose, and interprets language effect using an informational interview as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Dr. Deepa Malik's account of choosing possibility over remorse after paralysis, and her Paralympic silver at Rio 2016.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage above and answer the questions that follow.

1. In one sentence, state the TWO choices Dr. Malik says she faced after her surgery, and identify which one she chose.
2. Why does Dr. Malik describe the Rio 2016 silver medal as a 'breakthrough moment' rather than simply a 'victory'? Give one reason based on the passage.
items.visual_stimulus:
From the interview (pp.139–140):
“I had two choices—squander my life in remorse or transform it to a world of limitless possibilities. I love sports and had been a swimmer too, so I decided to switch to para-athletics. This is how my Paralympics journey began. My breakthrough moment came in the 2016 Rio Paralympic Games, when I secured the silver medal in the shot-put event. In hindsight, I feel it was a moment of personal victory and a step forward in changing perceptions.”

expected_elements: Names both choices: squandering life in remorse versus transforming it, choosing transformation.
Links 'breakthrough' to changing external perceptions, not only personal achievement.
Uses textual evidence (quoted phrase or paraphrase) to support each answer.
Distinguishes between individual victory and broader social significance.
Writes in complete sentences with appropriate formal register.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, evaluates authorial purpose, and interprets language effect using an informational interview as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Dr. Deepa Malik's account of choosing possibility over remorse after paralysis, and her Paralympic silver at Rio 2016.
items.item_stem: Dr. Deepa Malik states that Paralympics has 'the extraordinary ability to challenge stereotypes and change attitudes towards disability'. Evaluate this claim using at least TWO specific aspects of Dr. Malik's own life and advocacy work described in the interview. In your response, also assess whether the title 'The World of Limitless Possibilities' is an accurate representation of her philosophy, and justify your assessment.

expected_elements: Cites at least two specific examples: Rio silver, 'firsts', advocacy activities, or disability-awareness sessions.
Explains how each example challenges a named stereotype about disability or gender.
Directly addresses the title and connects it to Dr. Malik's stated philosophy ('ability beyond disability').
Provides a reasoned judgement on the title's accuracy, not merely asserts it is good.
Maintains a formal analytical register throughout the response.

items.source_lo: Student listens to an informational announcement and retrieves precise details using a listen-and-respond format.
items.source_context: World Inclusion Day school assembly announcement: venue, programmes, Interact Club staging, dance, panel discussion, closing song.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the World Inclusion Day assembly announcement. Choose the correct answer for each question.

1. The assembly is scheduled for:
2. Which group will present a staging on inclusion?

options.label: 1A
options.text: Friday, 11 October, at 9.00 a.m. in the school auditorium

options.label: 1B
options.text: Thursday, 10 October, at 10.00 a.m. in the school library

options.label: 1C
options.text: Thursday, 10 October, at 9.00 a.m. in the school auditorium

options.label: 1D
options.text: Wednesday, 9 October, at 10.00 a.m. in the school hall

options.label: 2A
options.text: Guest speakers at the panel discussion

what_each_option_reveals.1A: Errors in day — student may have counted forward one day incorrectly.
what_each_option_reveals.1B: Correct day but wrong time and wrong venue — student remembered one detail accurately but missed others.
what_each_option_reveals.1D: Confuses the day, time, and venue — likely a misheard detail from the announcement's opening.
what_each_option_reveals.2A: Student has reached past the staging to a later item on the programme — the guest speakers hold the panel discussion, which comes after the performances.
what_each_option_reveals.2C: Student has taken the assembly's opening — the Principal gives the welcome speech that the staging FOLLOWS, not the staging itself.
what_each_option_reveals.2D: The closest distractor, and the one worth discussing: the dance team does perform, on diversity and acceptance, but the announcement assigns the 'staging on inclusion' to the Interact Club.

items.item_stem: After listening to the World Inclusion Day announcement, a student claims: 'The assembly ends with a panel discussion featuring guest speakers, not a song.' Is this statement true or false? Write your verdict and give one detail from the announcement to support it.

options.text: The assembly ends with a panel discussion featuring guest speakers, not a song.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: False. The announcement states the event concludes with a song presented by students to nurture inclusive practices and collaboration; the panel discussion takes place before the closing song, not after it.

Asks at least one question about personal experience and one about challenges faced.
Listens to the interviewee's response before posing the next question.
Avoids reading from notes; speaks with reasonable fluency and eye contact.
Responds naturally to unexpected answers rather than following a rigid script.

items.item_stem: You are participating in a class debate on the motion: 'Disability is a unique strength, not a limitation.' Argue FOR the motion. Use Dr. Deepa Malik's story and at least one broader argument to support your position. Speak for one to two minutes.

References Dr. Malik's transformation from paralysis to para-athletics as evidence.
Offers at least one argument beyond Dr. Malik's case (e.g. systemic, philosophical, or personal).
Uses formal debate register: appropriate address, structured argument, confident delivery.

items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an editorial claiming that disability-awareness programmes in schools are 'a distraction from academic goals'. Write a letter to the editor (120–150 words) arguing against this view. Draw on the idea that such programmes build empathy, inclusion, and resilience — values that support academic and personal growth alike.

expected_elements: Follows the formal letter-to-editor format: address, date, salutation, body, closing, name.
Clearly states the position opposing the editorial's claim in the opening paragraph.
Provides at least two reasons or examples supporting inclusion programmes' educational value.
Uses formal, persuasive register with logical connectives (furthermore, however, therefore).
Concludes with a call to action or a strong restatement of the position.

items.item_stem: Match each sentence from Dr. Malik's interview with the function of the modal verb it contains.
items.visual_stimulus:
Sentence | Function of modal verb
Dr. Malik said she could hear the crowd cheering from the moment she entered the arena. | —
She told reporters she would continue to advocate for disability rights throughout her career. | —
In those early months after surgery, she felt she could not manage even a short swim. | —
She believed that young para-athletes should aim for international competitions, not only national ones. | —

answer_key.left: Dr. Malik said she could hear the crowd cheering from the moment she entered the arena.
She told reporters she would continue to advocate for disability rights throughout her career.
In those early months after surgery, she felt she could not manage even a short swim.
She believed that young para-athletes should aim for international competitions, not only national ones.

The sentences below are in direct speech. Rewrite each one in reported speech, making all necessary changes to pronouns, tense, and reporting verb. Write your answers in complete sentences.

items.item_stem: The Paralympics began as a small rehabilitation sports event at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in 1948 and has grown into one of the world's largest sporting competitions. Write a short response (4–6 sentences) explaining what this growth tells us about how the world's understanding of disability and athletic potential has changed over the decades.

expected_elements: Notes the contrast between the 1948 rehabilitation context and today's global competitive scale.
Links the growth of the Paralympics to changing social attitudes toward disability.
Uses at least one concrete detail (e.g. Rome 1960 as first official Paralympics, or inclusion in Olympic host cities).
Connects the historical shift to the chapter's theme of ability beyond disability.
Writes in a clear, analytical register rather than simply narrating events.

items.item_stem:
In a group of four, research ONE of the following topics and prepare a structured presentation to share with the class:
(a) Two lesser-known Paralympic sports (such as para equestrian or para rowing): cover the sport's rules, how it accommodates athletes with disabilities, and at least one notable competitor.
(b) Two Indian Paralympians who are not Dr. Deepa Malik: cover their sport, their disability category, a significant achievement, and the barriers they overcame.

Your presentation must include: one introductory slide, two slides on the history of the Paralympics, four to five slides on your chosen topic, and one concluding slide. Each group member must present at least one slide. Use appropriate images, colour schemes, and a balance of text and visuals.

expected_elements: Covers the required slide count and structure: introduction, history, topic, conclusion.
Content is accurate and drawn from at least two distinct sources (magazine, newspaper, or verified internet).
Each group member presents at least one slide with audible, clear delivery.
Slides balance text and images; design choices (colour, layout) support readability.
The conclusion connects the researched topic to the chapter's theme of limitless possibility or disability advocacy.
